_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-08.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed. Stray punctuation before marked words is trimmed, and Strong's tags that light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, are taken off as a stretch of words.

Then kept figures of speech were read again by two readers, a third settling any difference ("words re-read" counts them: those a sample showed at risk, such as wide spans, or those found only in the Hebrew or Greek that carry no tags): each kept as it was, cut to the words that carry the figure, or dropped ("words").

Strong's tags are also taken off any kept place whose tags light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, or whose roots light more words of the verse than there are tags, or, on a question or parallel lines, that were chosen for marked words since changed: such tags are a stretch of words, or name words no longer marked.

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

Then, after a review of the build checks, every kept place was checked again as the build now checks it: overlapping entries were joined, so the place marks the same words ("overlapping entries joined"), and any place the build would refuse was dropped ("refused on the later checks").
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.why: The Hebrew bim'od me'od ('muchness, muchness') plainly doubles the word for force, rendered 'exceedingly'. The mark 'I will make you exceedingly' takes in the verb; only 'exceedingly' carries the doubling. The tags sit on the two me'od.
Me'od me'od ('very, very') is a plain doubling for force, rendered 'exceedingly'. The mark 'became exceedingly' adds the verb; only 'exceedingly' should be marked. Tags are right.
Yom yom ('day after day') is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying 'every day'. It tells how often she spoke, not a word doubled for weight, so the figure is not plain.

Line 2 takes up 'a fruitful vine' from line 1 and goes a step further ('by a spring'), the pattern of climbing lines, not a word doubled in a row for force. The mark was the whole verse; line 3 does not take up words of line 2, so only lines 1 and 2 are marked, each as its own BSB poetry line.
Yom yom here means 'daily', what they gather each day: the ordinary distributive, not a doubling for force. The mark 'day' also lands on 'sixth day', which is not one of the doubled words.
Babboqer babboqer ('Every morning') is the plain Hebrew distributive for a daily routine. Nothing in the verse shows it doubled for weight.
Mizzeh ... mizzeh and mizzeh umizzeh mean 'on this side and on that', a set phrase of direction, not a word said twice for force. The marks 'the' and 'tabernacle to cover' carry no figure.
Babboqer babboqer ('every morning') only says how often Aaron burns incense. It is the ordinary distributive, not a doubling for force.
Mizzeh umizzeh ('front and back') is the set phrase 'on this side and on that', joined by 'and', not a word doubled for force. The mark 'back' is also only half the phrase.
Babboqer babboqer ('morning after morning') is the ordinary distributive 'each morning'; force is not plain from the doubling itself. The mark 'after morning' also leaves out the first 'morning'.
Mizzeh umizzeh ('on this side and that') is a measuring phrase, not a doubling for force, and the mark 'as well' does not render it at all.
The BSB reads only 'alternating the bells and pomegranates', so no doubled word shows, and the place has no tags. The Hebrew repetition describes a repeating pattern, not anything said for weight.
Beharot beharot in a law about skin marks reads as 'spots here and there', a distributive plural, not a word doubled for weight.
The BSB's 'I, even I' renders 'af-'ani ('also I'), which has only one 'I' in the Hebrew. The doubling is the translation's English, not a doubled word in the text.

Ya'an uveya'an ('because, even because') repeats the same word side by side, and the repetition has no grammatical or distributive use, only force. The Hebrew words shown make it plain; the BSB's one 'because' is the right word to mark, and the tags sit on both ya'an.

The marked BSB words "have been given exclusively" show no doubled word. The doubling (ne.tu.Nim ne.tu.Nim) is only in the Hebrew, and the place does not say so. Its tag H5414G also lands on the opening verb ve.na.ta.Tah, "Assign", which is not part of the figure, so the tags do not point only at the words that carry it.

Badderekh badderekh ('by the road, by the road') insists on keeping only to the highway, as 'We will not turn to the right or to the left' confirms. The marks took in the verb 'will stay' and a stray 'We'; 'on the main road' carries the doubling. Tags sit on the two derekh.
Me'at me'at ('little by little') is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying 'gradually', set against 'all at once'. It is not plainly a doubling for weight.
Shanah shanah ('each year') only says how often the tithe is set aside. It is the ordinary distributive, not a doubling for force.
Henah vahenah ('this way and that') is a set phrase of direction joined by 'and', rendered 'in any direction'. It is not a word doubled for force.
Jael's 'Come in, my lord. Come in' doubles the call with only 'my lord' between, to press Sisera, plain in the BSB. The mark was the whole verse; only the doubled call should be marked.

'to help the LORD, to help the LORD' plainly repeats the phrase in both the BSB and the Hebrew. The mark 'of the LORD' lands on 'the angel of the LORD' and the lone 'to help the LORD' duplicates part of the doubling; only the doubled phrase is kept. The tags are the roots of the doubled words.

The LORD's call 'Samuel! Samuel!' is a plain doubled name. The marks 'Samuel' and 'And Samuel' land on Samuel's answer, which is not part of the call, and are dropped. H8050G is the root of the doubled name.
Babboqer babboqer ('morning after morning') is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying 'every morning'. It shows the sadness went on, not a word doubled for weight, so in doubt it stays out.

Joab's "Far be it! ... Far be it from me" is cha.Li.lah cha.Li.lah side by side, and the BSB shows it too. The second span "be it from" drops "Far". A marked word may not repeat, so the two spans are "Far be it!" and "Far be it from me". Both H2486 tags are right.
'A.neh va.'A.nah ("where and where") is the idiom the BSB gives as "elsewhere". It is not a word doubled for force, and the marked "know" belongs to another construction.
mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh is the plain Hebrew for "on both sides". It describes the throne and is not a word doubled for weight.
mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh ("this side and that") tells where the lions stood. It describes and is not doubling for force.

"O altar, O altar" is a plain doubled address. The other marks ("the altar", "altar", "O altar") take in the narrative "cried out against the altar". The H4196 tags also light ha.miz.Be.ach in that narrative (word 2), so they come off.

Elijah's "Answer me, O LORD! Answer me" plainly doubles 'a.Ne.ni. The marks "O LORD" and "the LORD" (from "You, the LORD, are God") do not carry it. The H3068G tag lights both names, so the tags come off.
He.nah va.He.nah is the idiom "here and there" ("busy here and there"), not doubling for force. The mark is the whole verse.
He.nah va.He.nah, which the BSB gives as "to the right and to the left", describes the waters parting. It is not a word doubled for weight.
As in 2:8, He.nah va.He.nah ("to the right and to the left") describes the parting waters and is not doubling for force.
ge.Vim ge.Vim is the Hebrew way to say many ditches (BSB "full of ditches"). It is an idiom of number, not plainly a word doubled for force, so when in doubt it does not go live.
'A.neh va.'A.nah is the idiom the BSB gives as "anywhere". It is not doubling for force.
"My father, my father" is a plain doubled cry of grief, and the two 'a.Vi tags light only those words. The stray marks "father", "my father" and "the" are removed.
sha.Bat sha.Bat is the Hebrew for "every Sabbath", as the BSB gives it. It means each one in turn, not a word doubled for force.
"Peace, peace to you" plainly doubles sha.Lom. The marks "to you" and "to your" carry nothing and are removed. The H7965G tags light the peace words, the third being the same blessing carried on.

This is not one word said twice in a row. The second BSB line takes up "ascribe to the LORD" from the first and completes it with "glory and strength", which is climbing lines, as both readers proposed. The marks are now the two BSB lines.
ba.Bo.ker ba.Bo.ker is the Hebrew for "every morning", as the BSB gives it. It means each day in turn and is not emphasis.
mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh is the plain idiom for "on both sides" of the seat. It describes and is not doubling for force.
mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh ("one at either end of each step") tells where the lions stood. It is description, not emphasis.
ba.bo.ker ba.Bo.ker means "every morning" (with "every evening" beside it), a Hebrew way of saying each day in turn. It is not doubling for force.
The people's "Amen, Amen!" is a word doubled for solemn force, and both H0543 tags are right. The stray marks "Amen" and "Then" are removed.

The BSB's "How long, O LORD, how long?" doubles the words, but the Hebrew has 'ad-ma.Tai only once ("and You, O LORD, until when?"). The doubling is the translation's, not the verse's. A breaking off is not plain in the BSB either.

This is not one word said twice in a row. The second BSB line takes up "ascribe to the LORD" from the first and completes it with "glory and strength", which is climbing lines, as both readers proposed. The marks are now the two BSB lines; the title line is left out.

"Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy" plainly doubles cho.ne.ni, and the BSB shows it. The "O God" mark and its H0430G tag are on the address, not the doubled word. The tags cannot be cut back to only H2603A, so they come off.
places.words_why: The plea is plainly said twice for force: "Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy." The doubled words are "Have mercy" and "have mercy", so "on me" should not be lit.

places.why: "My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast" plainly doubles the clause. The marks are cut back to the two clauses, without the "O God" address. The H0430G tag lights that address, so the tags come off.

"Awake" calls two different hearers (my glory; harp and lyre), so it is not one word doubled for force. But two BSB lines plainly open with the same word, which is Like beginnings. The marks are now the two whole lines.
In "fulfill my vows day by day", yom yom is the ordinary Hebrew way to say "daily". No word is said twice for weight or feeling.

"Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You" repeats a whole line and adds "all", so it is a parallel line. It is not one word said twice in a row, and a reader would not see a doubled word here.
This is the same refrain as 67:3: "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You." A whole line is repeated with "all" added, which is a parallel line, not a doubled word.
In "who daily bears our burden", yom yom is the plain Hebrew idiom for "daily", not a doubling for force. The BSB shows no doubled word.
The BSB reads "have taunted ... and have mocked", two different words, and no Hebrew is shown. A reader cannot see a doubled word here.

The repeated nas'u neharot shows only in the Hebrew, and the tags wrongly light Yahweh, so they cannot stand. Without them the BSB's "floodwaters have risen ... rivers have raised ... seas lift up" shows no doubled word.
"God of vengeance, O God of vengeance" plainly doubles the title. The opening "O LORD," is outside the pair, so it is no longer marked.

"How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?" plainly doubles the cry. The marks are now only the two doubled phrases, without "O LORD". The tags go because they light Yahweh, and the BSB shows the figure without them.

"Not to us, O LORD, not to us" is a plain doubling. The marks are now only the two doubled phrases. The tags go because they light Yahweh and leave "to us" out, and the BSB shows the figure without them.

The Hebrew 'aleikhem 'aleikhem takes up "to you" so the blessing can reach "you and your children". That is not plainly a doubling for force. The H5921A tag also lights ve'al ("and to"), and without the tags the BSB's "give you increase, both you and your children" shows no doubling. When in doubt, drop.

Two BSB lines plainly open with "The right hand of the LORD", and each says something new. That is Like beginnings, not one word doubled. The marks are now the two lines instead of one stretch over the whole verse.
"Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy" plainly doubles the plea, in the BSB as well as the Hebrew. "O LORD" is no longer marked, and the tags go because they light Yahweh.
places.words_why: The cry is plainly doubled for force: "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy." Only the repeated "Have mercy" and "have mercy" carry the figure, so "on us" should not be lit.

places.why: "more than watchmen wait for the morning" is plainly said twice in a row. The mark now covers only the doubled words and leaves out the first line, "My soul waits for the Lord".

In the Hebrew, nachalah ends one line and is taken up to begin the next, which adds "to His people Israel". That is a take-up to extend the line, not plainly a word doubled for force, and the BSB varies the word ("inheritance", "heritage"). It is not a clear climb either. When in doubt, drop.
In "His delight day by day", yom yom is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for "daily", not a word doubled for weight.
In "watching daily at my doors", yom yom simply means "daily". The BSB rightly shows no doubled word.

In "It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine" a phrase is repeated, not a word said twice in a row, and "O Lemuel" stands between the two. The second "it is not for kings" also starts line 2 and carries its clause. The marked span runs across the poetry line break, so this is not plainly a doubled word.

"round and round it swirls" (sovev sovev) plainly doubles the word to show the endless circling. The H5437H tags light only that pair, not the earlier ve-sovev, so they stay. The extra mark "then turns" is a separate, earlier use and is dropped.

In the BSB each line plainly takes up a word of the line before (foxes, then little foxes; vineyards, then our vineyards) and goes a step further, to the vineyards now in bloom. That makes these climbing lines rather than a word doubled for force. The marks are now the three BSB lines. The tags were on the foxes pair alone, so they go.
"How beautiful you are, my darling— how very beautiful!" plainly says it twice for feeling. The marks now stop there and leave out the likenesses of doves and goats.
same form already on this verse (song-of-solomon-6-13-doubling-seen)
The tagged qav-qav is one reduplicated word (H6978) whose meaning is uncertain, and the BSB gives it as "powerful". A doubling for force is not plain, and the mark covered the whole verse.
This is the same qav-qav as 18:2: one reduplicated word of uncertain meaning, given in the BSB as "powerful". There is no plain doubling for force, and the mark covered the whole verse.

"You have enlarged the nation, O LORD; You have enlarged the nation" is a plain doubling. Both halves are the same words, so they are marked as one stretch. "O LORD" is no longer marked on its own. The tags go because they light Yahweh, and the BSB shows the figure without them.
same form already on this verse (isaiah-28-13-doubling-seen)
"morning after morning" (babboqer babboqer), set beside "by day and by night", is the Hebrew idiom for "every morning". It says how often, not a word doubled for force.
same form already on this verse (isaiah-48-11-doubling-seen)
"He awakens Me morning by morning" (babboqer babboqer) is the distributive idiom for "each morning". It gives frequency, not force.
"Awake, awake" ('uri 'uri) is a plain doubled cry, and the tags point at it. The later "Wake up" opens a new line and is a separate call, so the marked words are only the doubled pair.
"I, even I" plainly doubles the pronoun (anokhi anokhi), and the tags are right. "am" belongs to "am He" (hu') and is not part of the doubling.
"day after day" (yom yom) is the ordinary idiom for "daily". It says how often they seek, not a word doubled for force.
bo'rot bo'rot stand side by side, and the BSB shows the repetition, "cisterns— broken cisterns", which stresses that they are worthless. The tags are right, but the marked words were the whole verse.
The phrase is said three times in a row as an empty chant, and the BSB shows it plainly. The tags on heikhal and YHWH are the repeated words. The marked words should take in all three uses, not two.
"Peace, peace" plainly doubles shalom, and the two tags point at that word. "peace at all" is the separate shalom in "when there is no peace at all", so it is taken out of the marked words.

"iron— iron from the north" depends on how barzel barzel is read. The Hebrew can just as well mean "Can iron break northern iron and bronze?", with one iron the subject and the other the object. The second iron also names which iron. The doubling is not plain.

The BSB reads "a gadfly from the north is coming against her". No word is doubled, no Hebrew is shown, and the marked "against her" carries no figure. The note leans on a commentary and a disputed reading.
"Away, away! Do not touch us!" plainly doubles suru as an urgent cry. "Go away" is the earlier, separate suru in "Go away! Unclean!", so it is taken out of the marked words.
"engraved all around the wall" translates saviv saviv, the ordinary Hebrew adverb for "round about" in a description. It is not a word doubled for force.
bim'od me'od ("very, very") behind "You became very beautiful" doubles the word to make it stronger, and the tags point at it. Only "very" carries it, not "You became".

The BSB's "groan! Groan before their eyes" does put the word twice in a row, but the second "Groan" starts a new clause, and the Hebrew does not double it. The Hebrew has he'anach "groan", then "with breaking of loins and with bitterness", then te'anach "you will groan": one word in two forms with other words between. So the doubling in a row comes from the BSB's word order, not from the verse itself. That leaves it in doubt, so it fails.
"Turn! Turn from your evil ways!" plainly doubles shuvu, and the tags point at that word. "should turn" is the earlier, separate beshuv, so it is taken out of the marked words.
The BSB reads "Behold, I Myself will judge", so no word is doubled. In the Hebrew, hinneni ani is a suffix plus a pronoun, not the same word twice, and the marked words are the whole verse.
"He led me all around among them" translates saviv saviv, the ordinary idiom for "round about". It is not a doubling for force.
"a vast army" translates chayil gadol me'od me'od ("great, very, very"). The doubling makes the word stronger, and the tags are right. "vast" carries it, not "army".
"a wall surrounding the temple area" translates saviv saviv, the stock adverb for "all around" in a measured description. It is not a doubling for force.
"The gateway extended around to the gatepost" translates saviv saviv, the standard idiom in the temple measurements. Nothing is doubled for force.
"a pavement laid out all around the court" translates saviv saviv, an ordinary idiom in a description. It is not a doubling for force.
"windows all around" translates the idiom saviv saviv, not a doubling for force. The marked "like" belongs to "like the other windows" and has nothing to do with it.

In a list of gate measurements, sa.Viv sa.Viv is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying "all around" ("windows all around"). Nothing in the verse shows weight or feeling, so a reader would not see a word doubled for force without being told. The second mark, "it", is unrelated anyway. In doubt, so dropped.

"The porticoes around the inner court" is a bare measurement. The doubled sa.Viv is the usual idiom for "all around", with no force or feeling the verse shows. The mark also takes in "the inner court". Dropped.

"Windows all around" in a measuring list renders the stock idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv. The verse shows no weight or feeling, and the mark "It" ("It was fifty cubits long") has nothing to do with it. Dropped.
"It also had windows all around" uses the ordinary idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv in a technical description; nothing marks it out for weight. The mark "It" is a stray word. Dropped.

"Fastened all around the inside of the room" is a detail of the furnishings. sa.Viv sa.Viv here is the normal idiom for "all around", not a word said twice for force, and the verse gives no sign of emphasis. Dropped.

"Each side room around the temple was four cubits" is a measurement using the idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv (followed by a third, single sa.Viv). No weight or feeling is shown. The mark "of each" is also not the doubled word. Dropped.
"There were ledges all around the wall of the temple" is building description. sa.Viv sa.Viv is the stock way of saying "all around" and the verse does not show it said for force. Dropped.

le.Ma'.lah le.Ma'.lah here means "level by level, ever higher" ("widened at each successive level", "ascended by stages"), a stepwise description of the structure, not a word doubled for weight. The marks also stretch over whole phrases, and "as it rose upward" renders a single le.Ma'.lah. Dropped.
"A raised base all around it" is a measurement with the usual idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv. The verse shows no force or feeling, and the mark takes in "it", which is not part of the pair. Dropped.

"Twenty cubits wide all around the temple" is a plain measurement. The doubled sa.Viv (after a single one earlier in the verse) is the idiom for "all around", not emphasis a reader would see. Dropped.
"The open area was five cubits wide all around" uses sa.Viv sa.Viv as the ordinary expression for "all around" in a measurement. Nothing in the verse shows weight. Dropped.
"Five cubits thick all around" is a builder's measurement. sa.Viv sa.Viv is the normal idiom, and the verse does not show it doubled for force. Dropped.

"Overlaid with wood on all sides" renders the idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv in a list of fittings, with no force shown. The first mark, "all around" ("the galleries all around"), renders a single sa.Viv, so it is not doubled at all. Dropped.
"Spaced evenly around" renders the idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv in a technical description, with no weight shown. The only mark is "the", which carries nothing. Dropped.
"They were carved all the way around the temple" states how far the carving went, using the ordinary idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv. A reader would not see a word doubled for force. Dropped.
"He measured the area all around" is a plain report of measuring with the stock idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv. Nothing in the verse marks it out for weight. Dropped.
"It had a wall all around" uses the ordinary idiom sa.Viv sa.Viv. The verse shows no force at that word, and the mark "five" has nothing to do with it. Dropped.

"All its surrounding territory" renders sa.Viv sa.Viv, the usual way of saying "round about". The verse's weight falls on "most holy" and "this is the law of the temple", not on this idiom, and the mark also takes in "its". Dropped.

mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh, "from this side and from that", names two different sides joined by "and"; it is not one word said twice for force. The marks "will have the area" and "each side of the area formed by" miss it anyway. Dropped.

ba.Bo.ker ba.Bo.ker is the ordinary Hebrew way of saying "every morning" ("you are to offer it every morning"), a repeat that means each one in turn. The verse shows no weight or feeling beyond the daily rule. Dropped.
"Every morning" renders the same distributive idiom ba.Bo.ker ba.Bo.ker, not a word doubled for force. The mark also takes in "a grain offering". Dropped.

"The oil every morning as a regular burnt offering" uses ba.Bo.ker ba.Bo.ker to mean "each morning". It is a distributive idiom in a rule for offerings, not a doubling a reader would see as emphasis. Dropped.
"Along both banks" renders mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh, "on this side and on that": two sides joined by "and", not one word said twice in a row for force. The mark "along both" also takes in "along". Dropped.
"Along both banks of the river" renders mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh, "this side and that", which names two sides joined by "and". That is not a word doubled for weight. Dropped.
"On both sides of the holy portion" renders mi.Zeh u.mi.Zeh, two sides joined by "and" in a boundary description. It is not one word said twice for force. Dropped.

"I, even I, will tear them to pieces" renders 'a.Ni 'a.Ni (words 7-8), the pronoun doubled for force, and the tags are on those two words. The bare mark "I" could land on "For I am like a lion" (a different word, 'a.no.Khi) or on "I will carry them off", and "even I" adds nothing. So the only mark kept is "I, even I".

In "morning by morning" (ba.Bo.ker ba.Bo.ker) the word is repeated to mean each morning. The Hebrew and the English both use this ordinary pattern to say something happens regularly. Nothing in the verse shows the word doubled for weight or feeling, so the figure is not plain. When in doubt, the place stays out.

"Day and night they never stop saying: 'Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty'": hagios is said three times in a row (Greek words 25 to 27), so the repetition is plain and doubling is the right form. The mark "Holy, Holy" leaves out the third word, so the words become "Holy, Holy, Holy". The G0040G tags point at the repeated word, so they stay. A third G0040G tag is needed for the third hagios.

"calling in a loud voice, 'Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth'": ouai is said three times in a row (Greek words 12 to 14), so the repetition for force is plain. The mark "Woe! Woe" stops at two, so the words become "Woe! Woe! Woe". The G3759 tags point at the repeated word, so they stay. A third G3759 tag is needed for the third ouai.
